video_title: This Founder Raised $112M to Build Retail AI That Sells Like TikTok
gist: Zoe Wild, co-founder and CEO of Sequin, explains how its small, non-LLM ranking models use live in-session signals such as scroll speed, hover dwell and back-and-forth between products to lift retailer revenue, and argues that retailers cannot copy social-media recommender results without social-media data. The transcript does not mention the $112M raise from the title.

insights.claim: Sequin argues that classic search and relevance work, aimed at helping shoppers find things faster, is the wrong objective for commerce ranking. Its models instead try to influence behavior at a moment of high intent to lift basket size and average order value.
insights.speaker: Zoe Wild, Sequin co-founder
insights.so_what: Reframes e-commerce ranking vendors: the edge is in outcome-optimized ranking, not semantic retrieval quality.
insights.quote: We're trying to influence their behavior in a moment of time when they have high intent.

insights.claim: Semantic retrieval is largely a solved problem, with frontier labs doing it well, so on its own it is no longer an interesting research area. Commercial value now sits in behavior-influencing ranking.
insights.speaker: Zoe Wild, Sequin co-founder
insights.so_what: Retrieval and embedding quality is commoditizing; differentiation moves to objective choice and signals.

insights.claim: Modern recommenders at TikTok and Instagram no longer recommend content or help users find things. They shape what users want, which works because billions of people open the apps 10 to 21 times a day, producing huge behavioral data.
insights.speaker: Zoe Wild, Sequin co-founder
insights.so_what: Social platforms' conversion edge is a data-scale moat that retailers cannot copy by reading their papers.

insights.claim: Even very large retailers such as Wayfair and Priceline, with tens of billions of dollars in online transactions, are data-starved relative to social platforms because users are not addicted to their apps. This explains why imported social-media ranking methods underperform for them.
insights.speaker: Zoe Wild, Sequin co-founder
insights.so_what: The retail-ranking gap is a data-scarcity problem, which a vendor using in-session signals can claim to close.

insights.claim: Retail data scientists who replicate published social-media ranking papers often implement them successfully, but the methods fail to deliver the same outcomes because they lack the data those companies have. Sequin's pitch is delivering that lift without the data.
insights.speaker: Zoe Wild, Sequin co-founder
insights.so_what: Skepticism is warranted toward in-house recsys builds that copy big-tech papers.
insights.quote: It doesn't drive the same outcomes for you as it does for them because you don't have the data that they have.

insights.claim: Published big-tech ranking papers are watered-down versions of the real work, because scientists wait months for legal approval. Sequin says it has codified unpublished 'residual knowledge' from hires out of these firms into a proprietary harness library and knowledge base.
insights.speaker: Zoe Wild, Sequin co-founder
insights.so_what: The moat claimed is institutional know-how rather than model size; hard to verify externally.

themes.theme: In-session micro-signals and large event models

insights.claim: Sequin's models consume fine-grained live signals such as hovers, scroll speed, hover dwell time, and how many times a user goes back and forth between two products. Each user is treated as a collection of events in a session, with no identity, name or location needed.
insights.speaker: Zoe Wild, Sequin co-founder
insights.so_what: Session-only signals avoid cross-customer data sharing and identity, which has privacy and portability advantages.

insights.claim: Sequin's first product was a black-box model built on 'large event models', which generalize across human behavior event streams in real time the way LLMs generalize across text. They were followed by 'large mesh models', which are more relational and read many streams at once, and then hundreds of thousands of proprietary 'frontier ranking models'.
insights.speaker: Zoe Wild, Sequin co-founder
insights.so_what: Shows the architecture progression and the claim of large-scale proprietary model proliferation.

insights.claim: Serving requires digesting and transforming raw events in nanoseconds, passing them through hundreds of models, and returning re-ranked items in under 50 to 100 milliseconds at thousands of requests per second. Sequin built 'sequent ranking clusters' and a Rust backend to do it.
insights.speaker: Zoe Wild, Sequin co-founder
insights.so_what: The latency and infrastructure burden is a barrier to entry that helps explain why in-house builds struggle.

insights.claim: Sequin says its core backend could not have been built in Python and that it depends on Rust, whose open-source AI library support matured over the past 3 to 4 years. Python is used only for research and development.
insights.speaker: Zoe Wild, Sequin co-founder
insights.so_what: Rust is rising for ultra-low-latency ML serving, which is a tooling trend to watch.
insights.quote: I do not think we could have done it in Python.

insights.claim: Sequin does not use LLMs or generative AI. Its models use self-attention and many mixture-of-experts components, are far smaller than frontier models, and are specialized per domain such as ads, travel, retail and media. Generic giant embedding models are less useful for 2 to 3 token queries whose meaning differs by vertical.
insights.speaker: Zoe Wild, Sequin co-founder
insights.so_what: A profitable AI business is described as built on small specialized ranking models rather than LLMs.

insights.claim: Sequin deliberately avoids investing in generic multimodal representation learning of images and text, expecting it to be commoditized by frontier labs and open source. It is focused on the core ranking models and its evaluation harnesses.
insights.speaker: Zoe Wild, Sequin co-founder
insights.so_what: Treating perception layers as commoditizing is a view on where AI value does not accrue.

insights.claim: Time-series and sequence modeling mattered much more early on and is now only a small part of Sequin's stack. Human shopping behavior is less orderly than language and is interrupted by random events such as a barking dog.
insights.speaker: Zoe Wild, Sequin co-founder
insights.so_what: Counters the instinct to apply LLM-style sequence modeling directly to consumer behavior.

themes.theme: Business outcomes and what Sequin claims to deliver

insights.claim: Sequin claims it can lift basket size by small but consistent amounts, for example $12 per order, which it says can quadruple a customer's profit target for the year in under a month. It does not try to turn a $100 couch sale into a $500 one.
insights.speaker: Zoe Wild, Sequin co-founder
insights.so_what: The key claim is a 4x profit-target outcome from small per-order uplift, which is unverified here.

insights.claim: Sequin says it can raise ad revenue and organic revenue together, whereas ranking that optimizes ad clicks usually cuts conversion. Its method uses micro feedback such as scroll speed to show shoppers things they actually want.
insights.speaker: Zoe Wild, Sequin co-founder
insights.so_what: If true, it breaks the usual ads-versus-organic tradeoff for retail media.

insights.claim: Complementary-item ranking differs by page. On a product page it needs more diversity because the shopper has not committed, but on the add-to-cart page it should show accessories, for example tennis balls after a racket, rather than more of the same product.
insights.speaker: Zoe Wild, Sequin co-founder
insights.so_what: A concrete example of context-dependent re-ranking and the conversion cost of repeating the purchased category.

insights.claim: Sequin says it relies overwhelmingly on implicit feedback, which it has far more of than the explicit signals like thumbs up that teams usually depend on. It dismissed a major bank's transaction data as the least interesting data because 99% of users never convert.
insights.speaker: Zoe Wild, Sequin co-founder
insights.so_what: Value in behavioral data is in non-converting sessions, which transaction records miss.
insights.quote: I'm interested in the 99% of data you actually don't have.

insights.claim: Sequin's 'recursive' stack works like tail recursion, learning continuously with small modifications rather than retraining ranking models from scratch daily or hourly. It claims to compound gains faster at a fraction of the compute, and customers own the resulting models.
insights.speaker: Zoe Wild, Sequin co-founder
insights.so_what: Continuous incremental learning cuts compute cost and underpins the 'customers own the models' pitch.

insights.claim: Sequin built evaluation harnesses to define commercial ground truth, and offline evaluation must differ by vertical. High-ticket travel and furniture overlap, but ads differ because clicks translate straight to revenue.
insights.speaker: Zoe Wild, Sequin co-founder
insights.so_what: Evaluation against purchase outcomes rather than relevance proxies is the differentiator, and applies to any AI system.

insights.claim: Sequin embeds forward-deployed engineers at every customer, so it does not need customers' feedback data. Zoe Wild says it does not share customer data across customers and does not store user information.
insights.speaker: Zoe Wild, Sequin co-founder
insights.so_what: Forward-deployed model suggests a services-heavy go-to-market, and the privacy stance addresses surveillance critiques.

insights.claim: Wild rejects the 'surveillance capitalism' critique, saying Sequin does not chase users across sites and does not aim for addiction. It uses in-session intent only, like a store salesperson noticing which sofa you linger on, and she says gains are cents on the dollar per transaction.
insights.speaker: Zoe Wild, Sequin co-founder
insights.so_what: Regulatory and reputational risk is lower than for identity-based targeting, but the host's concern is only partly answered.
